papers.title: Sequalae and reversal of age-dependent alterations in mitochondrial dynamics via autophagy enhancement in reprogrammed human neurons.
papers.summary: This paper studies how reprogrammed human neurons (likely induced or transdifferentiated from aged donor cells) show age-related changes in mitochondrial shape, movement, and turnover. The researchers investigate whether boosting autophagy—the cell's process for clearing damaged organelles—can reverse these age-associated mitochondrial defects. The findings suggest that enhancing autophagy may restore youthful mitochondrial dynamics in aged neurons, offering insight into cellular rejuvenation strategies.
papers.why: This work directly informs the mechanistic link between autophagy/mitophagy and mitochondrial quality control in aging neurons, providing a cellular model and intervention strategy (autophagy enhancement) that could be tested or referenced in spatial transcriptomic/metabolomic studies of neuronal aging and interneuron vulnerability in the brain.

papers.title: Detection of Spatially Aberrant Cells in Spatial Transcriptomics Data by Conformal Prediction
papers.summary: This paper introduces a method that uses conformal prediction, a statistical framework for quantifying uncertainty, to identify cells in spatial transcriptomics data whose gene expression patterns are spatially anomalous compared to their neighbors. The approach provides statistically valid confidence measures for flagging outlier cells, which could represent technical artifacts or biologically meaningful rare states. This is a computational/methods paper focused on statistical detection rather than a specific biological application.
papers.why: This method could help identify spatially aberrant interneurons or perineuronal net-associated cells in spatial transcriptomics datasets with statistical confidence, supporting AI/deep learning-based spatial data analysis in the study of neuronal subpopulations.

papers.title: GraphTransformer-CoGNN: A two-stage dynamic graph learning framework for label-scarce cell-type annotation in spatial transcriptomics
papers.summary: This paper introduces a two-stage deep learning framework combining Graph Transformers and cooperative graph neural networks to classify cell types in spatial transcriptomics data when labeled training examples are limited. The method models cells as nodes in a graph, using spatial and gene expression relationships to propagate label information more accurately. This addresses a common bottleneck in spatial transcriptomics workflows where manual annotation is costly and scarce, especially for rare or complex cell populations.
papers.why: This tool could help accurately annotate interneuron subtypes and other rare cell populations in spatial transcriptomics datasets from brain tissue, which is directly relevant to studying mitophagy and perineuronal nets with limited ground-truth labels.

papers.title: PSSD: Progressive Spatial-Semantic Decoupling for Flow-Based Gene Expression Prediction from Histology Images.
papers.summary: PSSD is a new computational method that predicts gene expression levels directly from histology images by progressively separating spatial and semantic information using a flow-based generative model. This approach aims to improve the accuracy of linking tissue morphology visible in standard microscopy images to underlying gene activity patterns. It represents an advance in spatial transcriptomics prediction, potentially reducing the need for costly direct molecular measurements.
papers.why: This method could enable prediction of spatial gene expression patterns from histology images of brain tissue containing interneurons and perineuronal nets, complementing spatial transcriptomics workflows used in the mitophagy/autophagy project.
papers.figure: A figure showing predicted versus ground-truth spatial gene expression maps overlaid on histology images, demonstrating spatial accuracy across tissue regions.

papers.title: Targeting Mitochondria for Postoperative Cognitive Dysfunction: From Mechanisms to Therapeutics.
papers.summary: This paper reviews how mitochondrial dysfunction contributes to postoperative cognitive dysfunction (POCD), a common complication after surgery and anesthesia marked by memory and cognitive decline. It discusses mechanisms like impaired mitophagy, oxidative stress, and disrupted mitochondrial dynamics in neurons as drivers of POCD. The review also covers potential therapeutic strategies targeting mitochondria to prevent or treat this condition.

papers.title: The interaction mechanism investigation of Beclin-1 on mitochondrial ferroptosis and autophagy in doxorubicin-induced mice myocardial injury
papers.summary: This study investigates how the protein Beclin-1 interacts with mitochondrial ferroptosis (an iron-dependent form of cell death) and autophagy in a mouse model of doxorubicin-induced heart muscle damage. Doxorubicin is a chemotherapy drug known to cause cardiotoxicity, and the researchers explore the molecular pathways linking Beclin-1's autophagy-regulating role to mitochondrial ferroptosis processes. The abstract suggests findings that clarify how these two cell death/survival pathways intersect in cardiac tissue under drug-induced stress.
papers.why: While this paper focuses on cardiac tissue and ferroptosis rather than neurons, its detailed mechanistic exploration of Beclin-1's dual role in autophagy and mitochondrial regulation could offer transferable insights into mitophagy pathway crosstalk relevant to neuronal mitophagy research.

papers.title: TRPML1 inhibits ferroptosis in atherosclerotic foam cells by activating autophagy
papers.summary: This study looked at TRPML1, a lysosomal calcium channel, in foam cells found in atherosclerotic plaques. The researchers found that TRPML1 helps protect these cells from ferroptosis, a form of iron-dependent cell death, by promoting autophagy. This suggests TRPML1 could be a therapeutic target for reducing cell death in atherosclerosis.
papers.why: While this paper focuses on cardiovascular foam cells rather than neurons, the mechanistic link between TRPML1-mediated autophagy activation and protection against ferroptosis may offer transferable insights into autophagy/mitophagy regulatory pathways relevant to neuronal survival and lysosomal function in the brain.

papers.title: Urolithin B ameliorates post-myocardial infarction cardiac dysfunction via TREM1-mediated autophagy activation and pyroptosis inhibition.
papers.summary: This study looks at Urolithin B, a gut microbiome-derived compound, and its effects on heart function after a heart attack (myocardial infarction) in an animal model. The researchers found that Urolithin B helps the heart recover by activating autophagy (a cellular cleanup process) and blocking pyroptosis (an inflammatory form of cell death), acting through a protein called TREM1. Overall, the compound appeared to reduce cardiac damage and improve heart function following the infarction.
papers.why: While this paper focuses on cardiac tissue rather than the brain, the mechanistic link between autophagy activation and cell death regulation is conceptually relevant to mitophagy pathways being studied in neurons, though the direct applicability to interneurons or perineuronal nets is minimal.
